papers.title: FlexWAM: Learning Flexible Visual Routing for World Action Models
papers.summary: Humans dynamically adjust their reliance on sensory modalities across manipulation stages. Although existing World Action Models (WAMs) fuse multi-camera observations, they struggle to adapt their reliance on individual views based on the current observations. This raises a central question: how can the action expert integrate complementary visual evidence while prioritizing the views most relevant to the current action? FlexWAM addresses this challenge through three modules. First, we alternate within-view and cross-view attention to capture view-specific dynamics and complementary cues. For action prediction, View-Routed Action Attention uses an observation-conditioned router to prioritize relevant views. To calibrate routing, we train a critic using counterfactual view credit, estimated from action loss sensitivity upon suppressing each view's contribution to action attention. We evaluate FlexWAM with two video backbones on five challenging real-world manipulation tasks across two robot platforms. The two variants improve mean task success by 16.4 and 23.0 percentage points over the strongest baseline. Project website: https://flexwam.github.io/.

papers.title: TeleMultiStream: An Integrated Robot Teleoperation System with Low-Latency Multi-Stream Video Feedback
papers.summary: Training embodied-intelligence models requires large-scale, high-quality demonstration data. Robot teleoperation provides an important means of collecting these data. Low-latency teleoperation also helps human operators take control promptly and provide corrective demonstrations in DAgger-based interactive learning. This paper presents TeleMultiStream, a robot teleoperation system that combines multi-stream WebRTC video feedback with UDP pose downlink. The system supports heterogeneous video sources and uses buffer reuse, bounded queues, and native XR rendering to reduce processing and waiting. In wired-LAN ZED Mini tests, TeleMultiStream's software and high-performance hardware encoding modes achieved dominant-interval Glass-to-Glass latency medians of 60 and 66~ms, respectively. These medians were 26.8\% and 19.5\% lower than the 82-ms RobotVision-PC reference, respectively. At the lower tested resolutions, the two TeleMultiStream encoding modes provided comparable visual latency. Their respective medians in three-stream Configuration~1 were 72 and 66~ms. In the higher-resolution Configuration~2, high-performance hardware encoding outperformed software encoding in latency and CPU utilization. It reduced mean encoding time from 11.85 to 8.80~ms and the dominant-interval Glass-to-Glass median from 94 to 88~ms. Its CPU utilization was approximately 67\%, compared with 265\% for software encoding. During three-stream reception with high-performance hardware encoding, the mean corrected one-way UDP latencies at 100~Hz were 1.576 and 1.800~ms in Configurations~1 and~2, respectively. Mean estimated packet loss was 0.0033\% in both configurations. These results support responsive teleoperation for robot demonstration collection.

papers.title: MoMa-NMP: Scene-Scale Neural Motion Planning for Mobile Manipulators
papers.summary: Mobile manipulators operating in homes and other complex environments must coordinate their base and arm over long horizons, navigating around obstacles, through narrow passages, and between constrained workspaces. Neural motion planners can provide fast closed-loop planning from partial observations, but scaling them to room-sized environments is difficult because generating high-quality training trajectories is itself a challenging motion-planning problem. To address this, we introduce MoMa-DemoSmith, a demonstration-generation pipeline that separates the problem into global path discovery for large complex scenes and local motion refinement for collision avoidance. This key separation enables the generation of millions of challenging whole-body trajectories across our procedurally generated scenes. We train MoMa-NMP on these demonstrations through behavior cloning (BC) followed by privileged on-policy distillation, achieving 87.0% success on our simulation benchmark and 77.5% across 80 trials in unseen real-world scenes. See video results at https://adamhkan.com/moma-nmp/.

papers.title: SuperNav-1.5: Structured Spatial Memory For Agentic Navigation Systems
papers.summary: This paper addresses the challenge of scene-level memory design for efficient navigation across sessions and successive object goals. Recent methods commonly represent a scene using scene graphs or image--text records. However, dense scene-graph representations impose substantial reasoning and context overhead on multimodal large language models, while image--text records cannot be directly converted into executable geometric routes. To address these limitations, we propose SuperNav-1.5, an agentic navigation system equipped with a structured spatial memory constructed by the agent. The memory consists of an area-segmented occupancy map annotated with agent-maintained, map-grounded memory nodes. This map guides the agent toward unvisited areas and provides executable routes to known locations. For multi-session navigation, we introduce agent-guided relocalization, whereby the agent infers an area prior from current observations and stored memory records to constrain geometric matching and localize the robot within the stored map. Together, these designs enable efficient navigation across session and successive object goals. Experiments show that our method outperforms baselines on single-object, multi-object, and demand-driven navigation benchmarks, with particularly strong gains in path efficiency. Multi-session evaluation demonstrates that the constructed memory can be reused, while deployment on a real quadruped robot further shows the system's applicability. Project Page: https://zju3dv.github.io/SuperNav-1.5/

papers.title: UnderGrasp: Envelopment-Oriented Grasp Refinement for an Underactuated Gripper
papers.summary: Underactuated grippers can form enveloping grasps through passive compliance, while the terminal pose and single width predicted by generic grasp generators do not fully capture the approach-closure process. Conventional collision filtering also struggles to distinguish harmful interference from acceptable contact. We present UnderGrasp, a post-hoc grasp refinement and evaluation framework for an underactuated gripper that reuses grasp candidates and quality priors from a frozen generator. The model jointly encodes the target, local environment, support surface, and approach-path geometry to propose diverse combinations of insertion depth, pre-grasp width, and target closing width for each candidate. These actions are ranked by combining separately predicted envelopment and interaction quality with upstream priors, balancing grasp feasibility, envelopment, and scene disturbance rather than rejecting all environmental contact. The back end is trained solely on configuration and interaction labels generated by gripper-specific simulations, without real-robot grasp labels. Real-robot experiments with an underactuated gripper show that UnderGrasp improves the overall success rate (SR) and the envelopment rate (ER) among successful grasps from 0.55/0.12 to 0.82/0.55 with AnyGrasp, and from 0.42/0.08 to 0.65/0.36 with GraspNet. In contrast, increasing the fixed insertion depth to 40 mm improves ER to 0.35 but reduces SR to 0.52, supporting the value of adaptive refinement. For trials involving target or environmental contact during approach, the conditional success rates increase from 0.36 to 0.89 and from 0.25 to 0.86, respectively, demonstrating more reliable execution under contact. papers.title: World Models and the Law
papers.summary: Current AI may have a model of how we use human language, but this does not translate into a reliable representation of physical reality. World models promise to fill this gap by learning how an environment changes over time and predicting the consequences of an action, and they are already used to steer robots and generate explorable worlds. This article asks how AI regulation in three major legal contexts, the European Union, California, and China, copes with the distinctive challenges they raise. I propose a definition and a taxonomy of world models based on who or what acts on their predictions, and identify the risks of misplaced reliance on them. I argue that existing rules tend to cover world models but leave three questions open, i.e., action provenance, trajectory validity, and the weight of simulated evidence, and recommend ways to fill these gaps.

papers.title: ProMix: Efficient Data Mixture Optimization for Robotic Imitation via Proxy-Reference DRO
papers.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models excel in open-world manipulation, yet their performance often saturates when training data are naively pooled across heterogeneous robots, tasks, and environments. Distributionally robust data mixture optimization, exemplified by Re-Mix, can recover much of this performance, but its weight search requires training full-scale policies twice on the entire corpus, placing it out of reach for most laboratories. We present ProMix, a compute-efficient instantiation of the proxy-reference DRO recipe for robotic imitation learning: a 15M-parameter proxy learns per-domain sampling weights by minimizing worst-case excess loss against a frozen reference model, and the learned weights transfer, without re-tuning, to VLA backbones up to 7B parameters. papers.title: Arcadian: Open-Source Humanoid Ecosystem for Accessible and Customizable Research and Education
papers.summary: Reproducing and modifying a meter-scale humanoid remains challenging for research and teaching groups with limited fabrication resources and engineering support. This paper presents Arcadian, an open-source humanoid ecosystem that offers accessible and customizable humanoid hardware and software with community support. Arcadian aims to strike a balance among cost-effectiveness, structural durability, and full customizability, lowering the barrier to entry for research and education. Specifically, this meter-scale humanoid adopts metal-embedded 3D printing to achieve a high strength-to-cost ratio, eliminating the need for computer numerical control (CNC) machining while retaining design flexibility. Extensive simulation and hardware tests validate the design: a reinforcement-learning (RL) locomotion policy trained in simulation transfers to the hardware, and a virtual reality (VR) teleoperation interface drives both arms for simple manipulation tasks. The robot is around one meter tall and costs approximately $6,800 to build. All computer-aided design (CAD) models, the bill of materials, assembly documentation, and training and deployment code are publicly released, distributed through Tnkr.ai and MakerWorld and supported by a Discord server and a project forum through which community feedback informs design updates. The ecosystem resources are available at https://anonymous-humanoid.gitbook.io/docs.

papers.title: World Models Are the Right Foundation for Simulating Mars Terraforming
papers.summary: Terraforming Mars is a long-horizon, action-conditioned control problem that requires predicting atmospheric responses to interventions over centuries to identify effective policies. This position paper argues that physics-regularized recurrent state-space world models are the most promising foundation for this setting. Data-driven climate emulators lack action-conditioning, and physics-based general circulation models (GCMs) are too expensive for policy search. Among learned world models, recurrent state-space architectures with physics constraints are better suited than transformer-based alternatives: they provide native uncertainty quantification through their stochastic-deterministic decomposition, remain stable under sparse non-terrestrial training data, and enforce physical consistency at each rollout step. To make this position concrete, we describe a potential architecture combining JEPA-inspired latent encoding, universal differential equation constraints, and a Dreamer-lineage planning head. We also introduce MarsWorld, an open benchmark proposal for intervention-conditioned planetary world models, and discuss broader implications and objections.

papers.title: Ego2Wrist: Bootstrapping Wrist-View Synthesis from Egocentric Video
papers.summary: Wrist cameras provide an action-centric view that is directly relevant to robot manipulation. However, collecting human wrist-camera videos at scale is challenging due to cumbersome setups that can interfere with natural hand movements. In contrast, head-mounted human egocentric videos are much easier to scale. We introduce Ego2Wrist, which synthesizes synchronized wrist-camera views from human egocentric videos and task descriptions. Trained on approximately 940 hours of paired head- and wrist-camera recordings, Ego2Wrist jointly generates three views. To evaluate generated wrist views without ground truth, we propose hand-centric cross-view consistency (HCC), which measures consistency between generated wrist views and corresponding hand regions in the input head view. HCC ranks model checkpoints comparably to ground-truth-based LPIPS, and human evaluators prefer HCC-selected generations in 77% of responses. Evaluated on four datasets, Ego2Wrist outperforms fine-tuned WorldWander, reducing LPIPS by 28% and receiving human preference in 76% of responses. More importantly, HCC facilitates recursive self-improvement on in-the-wild egocentric videos by selecting generated wrist views for further training. Generation quality progressively improves over three rounds. These results demonstrate a scalable approach to generating real-world wrist-view human manipulation videos for robot policy training.
